utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness? Then can the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I -- yes, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I just note for the record that the witness did receive a 90(E) admonishment previously in the Karadzic case, and we believe it would also be appropriate in the present case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It always depends on what kind of questions you will put to the witness. If we come at a point where you consider, either Defence or Prosecution, it would be wise to issue such a warning or rather explain to the witness what his rights are, then we'll do that. Meanwhile, in relation to Witness Indjic: Four notebooks were handed over to the Registry by Witness Indjic on the 5th of September of this year. They have been given to Chamber staff. The Chamber has not read any of the notebooks. Rather, it prefers that copies are made available to the parties and that the parties then make any further submissions as necessary. Accordingly, the Chamber instructs the Registry to make copies of the notes and share those copies with the parties, and the Chamber will not read them for the time being and will then await further submissions from the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujasin, I presume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make the solemn declaration. The text is handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vujasin. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, you will first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to speak slowly for the record and give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I'm Mihajlo Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, at one point in time, did you give a statement in writing to the Defence of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please take a look at 1D04072 in e-court. That is its 65 ter number. Could we please take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, is this your signature? And the date on the left-hand side, was it written in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When preparing for the procedure in courtroom today, I told you about this and now I'm going to ask you. When you took this solemn declaration here in this courtroom today and if you were to be asked the same questions as those contained in this statement, would you answer the same way?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I was fully aware of all of that. I would say the same things, yes, today. I have to say, however, there are a few grammatical mistakes, but on the whole it remains as it had been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to tender the statement of Witness Mihajlo Vujasin into evidence, 1D04072 being its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, in general we don't have an objection to the admission of the statement. However, I do not know yet which associated exhibits are going to be tendered, and there are quite a lot, and that could impact parts of the statement, so if we could leave it MFI'd until we know what associated exhibits are being tendered exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any problem with that? Of course, many paragraphs lose all probative value if the associated exhibits are not admitted, but perhaps it would be not too bad to, for the time being, MFI this statement so that we can deal with it in a consolidated way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Observing the instructions you provided, my plan was to reduce the list of exhibits so we're only going to tender nine documents along with this statement; that is to say, those that are derived from this witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, the number to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4072 receives D641.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D641 is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read out Mr. Mihajlo Vujasin's summary or rather the summary of his statement. It says that as a professional military man, he was serving at the air base in Rajlovac when the war broke out. After the JNA left the BiH, he held many responsible duties from deputy commander of the Rajlovac Brigade up until the 16th of September, 1992, when he took over as chief of engineering in the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and he remained in that position until the end of the war. In his statement, he speaks of the strategy of the SRK for Sarajevo pointing out that his role was a defensive one except for certain improvements in tactical positions from time to time. The task was the blockade of the 1st Corps of the BH Army and rendering it impossible to have it used at other front lines in the BiH. The BiH Army was in that area with its units at dominant features as related to Rajlovac, and the position of his units which was used for constant activity against military and civilian targets within Rajlovac and the surrounding Serb towns and villages. Neither he nor his brigade ever received any orders in writing or orally from higher commands to attack civilians in town or means of public transportation either using snipers or any other weapons, although they knew that civilian facilities were being abused for military purposes by the units of the BH Army. Humanitarian aid in Sarajevo passed through Rajlovac as well and was not stopped in any way. Also, the gas supply for the city of Sarajevo partly went through the area of the Rajlovac Brigade and that also continued. He never received orders for that to be stopped. He testifies about being present at the Nisici when the air bomb was being tested and also he says that he has no concrete knowledge about the characteristics and use of air bombs. He speaks about the attitude of the VRS towards paramilitary formations in the area of responsibility of his brigade, and he claims that the position of the command of the VRS towards the existence of paramilitary units was negative and they had orders to have these formations either expelled or placed under a single command. Finally, he testifies about the VRS, specifically his unit, and their relations with the civilian authorities in Rajlovac saying that these relations were not very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, now I'm just going to put a few questions to you that are based on this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we still have D641 on the screen, I would like us to focus on paragraph 5 of this statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- where you say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, in B/C/S could we move on to the next page? In English it's fine because I'm just going to be referring to the first sentence in paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 you say that: "The recruitment of personnel for the air force base war units had been carried out on a voluntary basis and two units had been formed by Serbian volunteers and one by Muslim." I'd like to ask you what you meant by this in your statement when you say that this was carried out on a voluntary basis, that was how personnel were recruited?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: It's very hard. Very hard question, very hard answer. But it would boil down to the following: First of all, the army as an army, it has its peacetime composition and it's wartime composition, but in war units are manned through the Ministry of Defence; that is to say, through municipalities, through regular channels. When mobilisation is carried out, some people did not respond. Primarily it was Muslims. And quite a few Serbs also had a negative attitude. They were saying, "You're only calling us up and there are no Muslims. So they are preparing for war." And this was already March, April, the beginning of 1992, that is to say the beginning of the war. I remember that full well, these call-up papers. A few people did come, Muslims, and we talked to them. There was no training anymore. This was just a conversation. And we said, "What's up?" And they said, "We have no approval. Whatever is happening is negative." Even the command knew about this, Belgrade knew about this, the Main Staff knew about this, and the army knew that it was impossible to man units through regular channels. And then there was this document that was adopted to do this on a voluntary basis. What does that mean? Whoever comes is then manning these wartime units. Specifically, the tasks are those like those of the former JNA --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like you to ask you to speak a bit slower for the transcript and also if you could be a bit more specific. Just a bit slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not only to be slower in speaking but to make a pause between question and answer because the interpreters need more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, I will stop you there for a second. I would like us to be a bit more specific here. According to what you just said, did people turn up from among the Bosniaks or the Croats who joined the JNA at that time on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: We were not able to form the JNA troops so then the decision was made to proceed on a voluntary basis, and then what happened is that the units who were from that area, they would come to join the army if the army was staying there. At that time we didn't know if the troops would be staying there or not. There was no decision. So for the most part you had Serb units, members of the units who were Serbs. But they were not the ones either who were there according to the wartime disposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I really must pay attention to the transcript so please understand why I'm making these brief pauses. Let us now look at paragraph 21 of your statement, D641, where you speak about handing over control of the airport to the UN, the airport in Sarajevo. And you say that you were in the position to hear that General Mladic ordered that not a single bullet be fired on the airport and that the airport be surrendered to the UN, and that this decision was taken in a negative way by the people. Could you please tell us in a couple of words, first of all, why did the people understand this in a negative way, the people in the area other than the fact that they were staying -- or they would remain in a double encirclement?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: When the blockade was lifted, when the people were divided, practically, after that it was not possible for either of them to leave their areas of responsibility. So what is negative there? The negative thing is that that area of the territory from Hadzici to Ilidza, Vogosca, Rajlovac, and Ilijas was cut off. Those people found themselves in an encirclement, they were in an enclave and were not able to survive in that area unless they could communicate freely in trade, in economic terms, so with the hand-over of the airport that possibility was ruled out. Once the airport was handed over, the people then were in that position and they didn't want to accept that. So it had a negative effect. There were even rebellions against that. The problem is that nobody asked those people anything from that area, not the president of the municipality or the senior officers of the army, so that was that. Then it was necessary to calm the people down and to get them to accept this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you said that General Mladic ordered that even in spite of that not a single bullet ought to be fired, could you please tell the Court when did you hear this? Did you hear it directly from General Mladic or did you have it conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: In the meantime, there was a meeting convened in Lukavica with representatives of the army from that area expected to attend the meeting. I was at the meeting representing the Rajlovac Brigade, I think there were about 20 or 25 of us there. Among other things, the political situation was discussed, what was happening, what the reasons were, and the senior organs decided to hand-over the airport. I did not agree with that. I thought that that was not a good idea. But of course we had to respect the decision of the government of Republic of Serbia that not a single bullet could be fired at the airport, so we were in a unenviable situation that we were placed in and were placed in the position that you could not fire at anything that had to do with the airport. And this caused a lot of problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at paragraph 23 and could we please look at the next page in the English version because that part is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'd like to get clarity on the question that you just put. You asked the question whether he heard Mr. Mladic give this order directly, and he says he went to a meeting and the leaders of -- there was a meeting and the leadership decided on this decision. And then he says that he felt he must respect a government decision. I'm not sure what -- he's not answering whether he heard this from Mr. Mladic, or was it made by this meeting that was meeting there, or was it made by the government and relayed to this meeting. Can you please clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is precisely what I wanted to do and that's why I wanted us to look at the next part of 23. Very well, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, did you hear that directly from Mr. Mladic or not?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: At this meeting, there were no civilians present. No civilian organs. It was just attended by senior officers, non-commissioned ones or active senior officials, so I heard it from him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now could you please look at this paragraph 23 where you say that General Mladic organised a meeting of all representatives of the brigade in Lukavica. You attended this meeting personally representing the Rajlovac Brigade and you note the words that General Mladic uttered on that occasion. My question is precisely at that meeting that you refer to in paragraph 23, was there also any discussion about what you have just said that General Mladic said?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, that did happen at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you to look at paragraph 49, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is document D641.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where you say that you had information that Serb civilians were not permitted to leave the city of Sarajevo. Could you tell us in a little bit more detail what this information was that you had? Why were Serb civilians not allowed to leave the city of Sarajevo which at that point in time was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Well, that problem is a very complex one. But actually, the barricades that were placed at the checkpoints on the roads between Serbs and Muslims, between the entrances and exits to the town, you had Serb barricades and then Muslim barricades. And then you had buildings, people could not pass the barricades without problems or without any, let us say, difficulties. Serbs from Sarajevo could not do that due to -- I know this because in Serb territory, specifically in my area, in Rajlovac, women were left behind and the rest of their family was in town, so they could not leave the town and go in this direction in any way. So, however, when the conflict escalated, then it got even worse. So it had not then, as we say, started to boil yet. So this is what happened there, certain groups used this situation. So for vast compensation in money they would let people go from the town into Serb territory. So, now, somebody comes, everybody hugs them, kisses them, and then they say how much did you pay for it? That was a very high price that they would pay for it. It was not an organised thing. It was actually very difficult to communicate between the sides unless it was organised. I tried to allow without any problems from our side to make this possible, and later I had problems with all the civilian organs and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what knowledge do you have as to the reasons why the authorities, the Muslim authorities, did not permit this flow of civilian citizens?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I think that the main reason was for one side to be accused and the other not. We had a multi-ethnic situation here saying that we have Serbs, Croats, and so on here, depending on the area of responsibility, and then you would present that to the international community, that they were the only ones that were in the right. They tried to show that their position was the only one that was proper and correct and no one else's, so it was necessary to show the international community that they were multi-ethnic. So this turned out the way it did later, 1991, 1992, everybody who came out did that under stress. And they came out like living skeletons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now look at paragraph 61 of your statement where you say -- when you're describing the relations with the civilian authorities during the period that you were in Rajlovac, that you had a bad relationship with the civilian authorities at the local level --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting, Mr. Stojanovic, but this was one of the paragraphs that actually the Prosecution had some concern about, and I think it would be most fair to alert Mr. Stojanovic to our concern before asking questions on it. In this paragraph there is reference to a statement of a Jovo Bozic being shown to the witness, and it appears unclear, actually, what the witness is referring to in the text of the paragraph, paragraph 61. I just want to alert the Chamber and the Defence that this statement is an RS SDB statement taken on 17 December 1992, and it is uploaded and available under Mladic 65 ter 10 -- excuse me 16018. I just wanted to put that on the record. Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that we will not have any problems in relation to that and that is why I would like to present a document that I would like to address that on. So I don't think that there's any need to look at this document. We take the caution on board, unless you believe it's necessary. I believe that there's no need and I did go through this with the witness. With your leave, Your Honours, I would continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, sir, Mr. Vujasin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it would be only fair to the Chamber and the opposing party that you put the right 65 ter number on the record in relation to this document, the right 65 ter number in the Mladic case. I think this is your obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And I want to show the document from the case under the 65 ter number if I understood you correctly. I do want to present that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I earlier then must have misunderstood you, that there was no need to show it to the witness. But please then proceed and take care that the 65 ter number which is valid in this case is clearly on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and then before I put the question, I propose that we look at that document, the 65 ter document. Can we look at 1D04096.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's number -- I'm a bit lost. Mr. Weber, you gave another number. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- do we have this same statement twice in the e-court system or -- because Mr. Stojanovic now comes with a --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, this appears to be a different document than the one that I have down as being associated from the Karadzic case. I do not believe that this is a statement from Mr. Bozic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. This isn't -- Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us whether you are living under the impression that this is the same document as the document referred to in paragraph 61 of the statement or is it a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to create any more confusion. This document in paragraph 61 marked as 65 ter number is from the Karadzic case. We did not place it on the list of potential exhibits that we wanted to use in the Mladic case. The document is not on our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then I take it that you first are seeking permission to have it on your 65 ter list, is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm not planning to use the document at all. It's not on our list, so I wasn't even planning to use it with the witness. I was going to use this other document that speaks about the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you say you're not going to use it with the witness and you put it on our screens, I mean what's -- it's rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but when you talk about a document or the document, could you always clearly indicate what document we have on our screen at this moment, a document. Is this the document that you said is not on your 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document that you have on your screen is on our 65 ter list and has the number 1D04096.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And is this document referred to anywhere in this statement as it was taken for the purposes of the Karadzic case? Or is it not to be found anywhere in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is mentioned in the first sentence of paragraph 61 of the witness statement. However, it is not referred to. It is the event itself that is referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. One second, please. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you said the document is mentioned in the first sentence of paragraph 61 which is not true. The first sentence doesn't mention any document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry if I said document, Your Honours. I wanted to say event, the event that this document speaks of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you corrected yourself. After you had said that the document was mentioned, you then said it's the event itself. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, according to our checks, and there were a lot of documents, and so if Mr. Stojanovic could maybe confirm this would be appreciated. I had it down, this document that's on the screen, as being associated to paragraph 85 of the statement which is towards the end. And that's just the information that I have so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, first of all, I have difficulties in finding that in paragraph 61 an event is described, it's rather a situation, I would say, than an event. Second, Mr. Weber suggests to you that the document which you are looking at at this moment may be the same as the document referred to in paragraph 85 of the statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Also in paragraph 85 that gives comments on all the documents that the Karadzic Defence tendered, and my plan is to reduce that in accordance with the instructions that I have received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You want to introduce -- well, we now know that the document which is on our screen now is corresponding with 1D8447 in the Karadzic case and that you want to put questions to the witness. Please do so. It would have been better to have done the same without creating so much confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, just for my own clarity, are we to understand that 65 ter 17258 has been removed completely from the evidence which is what you mentioned in paragraph 61?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We haven't placed that document in our list and we do not plan to use that document from the Karadzic case at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's mentioned in the statement, so are we deleting it from the statement? Thank you. And are we to understand then that 1D04096 is not the same thing as 16018 which was mentioned by Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it is not the same. It corresponds to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that 16018 would correspond with the Bozic statement as referred to in paragraph 61, Mr. Weber. That is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You confirmed that. That is now off the list, which means that the person of the statement starting with: "I was shown the statement of Rajlovac SO president ..." et cetera, that that is -- should be the redacted because you are not using that document. Therefore, all the comments on what the document tells us are without probative value. Therefore, Mr. Stojanovic, you would have to make a new version of the statement. Then we are now moving on. You are showing to the witness the document which is referred to in paragraph 85 and which was in the Karadzic case known as 1D8447 and which is in this case known as 1D04096. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vujasin, we've corrected this misunderstanding concerning numbers. This is what I'd like to ask you now. Please focus on this first sentence of paragraph 61. This is where you say -- actually, it's not on the screen anymore. But if you remember, you were saying that you had poor relations with the civilian authorities at local level because they had unrealistic expectations of the brigade and demanded more than the brigade was able to do. What was all of that about?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: First of all, may I say that the municipality of Rajlovac was established quite late in February that year and it came to include certain territories. Everybody wanted to be the boss in his own land. So, the unit that was formed belatedly was supposed to free the entire territory; that is to say, it should be free so that organs of authority could be established as deemed best. However, this could not have been done overnight simply by using a pen and paper. And now the authorities, Bozic and everybody else, Rajlovac was strong, economically strong because there were factories there, companies, 13, 14 state-owned companies --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So a lot of these facilities existed there and you just try to liberate the area where the municipality was, and then the conflict would be over as far as they were concerned. So pressure was brought to bear against people who were in Rajlovac, I mean women, children, refugees, to have this resolved, but the main thing was to resolve Sokolje Brijesce, Brijesko Brdjo, Zabrdje, that area. I mean, that's included by the municipality and that is land that belongs to this municipality, and this was unrealistic. These were unrealistic demands, and these unrealistic demands meant the use of force, major sacrifices, major everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I really have to stop you here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For my clarity, sir, Mr. Vujasin, you said the municipality was formed in February of that year. Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, did you have problems with members of your unit as well precisely because of that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: First of all, in the unit itself, I had problems. The people who were there, I had problems with them. And also with the municipality. When I say the municipality, the civilian structures of power, the SDS. Let's free this and then we're done. So that called for major sacrifices.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: So I tried, I mean, not to meet their demands but according to the situation, to preserve what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this document - and I would kindly ask you to take a look at it. It says, among other things, that a group of dissatisfied soldiers asked for the dismissal of the commander of the Rajlovac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Direct us where you are reading, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 3 of this document, Your Honour. The second and third lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It says that they demanded the dismissal of the commander of the Rajlovac Brigade, Lieutenant-Colonel Golijanin, and the Chief of Staff Captain First-Class Mihajlo Vujasin. Then the reasons are referred to why this demand is being made to have them dismissed. It says among other things, that soldiers were not protected and that they were exposed on a daily basis to fire from Sokolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we please move on to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This fire came from the Green Berets. In a word, the mentioned group demanded that Sokolje be taken and cleansed as simply as possible. The reasons mentioned here, did they correspond to the problem that you refer to when speaking of your relations with the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, that coincides. That's correct. So nothing was, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vujasin, I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Your Honour, I would now like to suggest that we admit a completely different abbreviated list of exhibits. So I would like to tender three maps that the witness marked and that are marked as follows: 65 ter 1D03109, 1D03110, 1D04095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it anywhere in the statement, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, they have been mentioned. I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 22 of this witness's statement in view of all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned three documents. Could you tell us where we find which document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In paragraph 22, the document 1D8445 has been mentioned. That is its Karadzic 65 ter number. 1D03110 would be its number in our case. And then the document in paragraph 22 that is marked as 1D8445A which corresponds to our document 1D04095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then there's still one missing. Where's the third one to be found?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third one, let me just take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe the third one is in paragraph 4. And the Prosecution has no objection to admission of the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D8444 in paragraph 4 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that corresponds with 1D03109. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It corresponds with document 1D03109. That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a simple "yes" therefore would have done. Mr. Stojanovic, we have now the three maps. Anything else you want to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a list, a list, a table of concordance?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the list that we provided to the Prosecution as well in relation to the documents that we are going to be using as associated exhibits when questioning this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you provide it to Chamber staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point, I have to admit that I'm not sure. This was done by the case manager. I think the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We only received annex B to your 65 ter motion with the associated exhibits as you pointed out and there we see also some 65 ter numbers from the Karadzic case. But this is not really a list of concordance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do we know what list -- what numbers exactly -- let me just ask -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, Madam Registrar shows me now a document with at the bottom, the date the 16th of September, 2014, whereas the Chamber has received a list which has some similarity but on which we find the date the 5th of September, 2014. May I take it that the 16th of September list is the one you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that's right, Your Honour. And I think that in that list you have the information from the Karadzic case, 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm informed now that Madam Registrar, and that explains the date on the bottom of it, has made a new printout. When did you provide what list most recently, a list on which you wish to rely and to whom did you provide that? And perhaps you already indicate to us how many documents are listed on that list. So the list you want to use, how many documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a total of 32 documents and there's the witness statement. According to the suggestions we received, I have reduced this and I am tendering a total of nine documents from this list and I would like to highlight that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where is the list of the nine documents you want to tender? Or is there no such list? Then make it very quickly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no separate list, Your Honour. These nine are from this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Has the Prosecution received notice of which nine you wanted to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have the 32. All I need to know is which are the nine, so if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- narrow it down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, already during your examination of the witness, you used 25 minutes for questions and 16 minutes were wasted with clarifying chaotic presentation. Now, here more or less the same happens. Apparently we have to look from a document -- let's go through that document very quickly. The first one you want to tender is -- I've seen the first two 1D03109, we have dealt with that one. That's a map marked. The next one is 1D03110, that one we have dealt with as well. And we have -- well, what's the next one on your list you want to tender? What's the next one on this list you want to tender? I know that there's a third one that appears further down on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Which one do you want to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04082. That's its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 82. 1D04082, is that -- that is the 65 ter number in the Mladic case or by the commander of the -- Vogosca Operations Group?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now where do we find this document in this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is referred to in the statement in paragraph -- just one moment, please. I'm going to tell you right away, Your Honours. In paragraph -- in paragraph 74 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you now know what we need. We need the 65 ter numbers under which the nine documents you want to tender are uploaded in the Mladic case. We need the corresponding 65 ter numbers from the Karadzic case and the paragraph in which that document is referred to by the witness. And you produce that list within the next 20 minutes, I would say, we take a break, and would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why not do it yourself? Why do we have to insist on this chaotic counter-productive way of proceeding? We expect such a list in 20 minutes, without mistakes, containing all the information I just referred to, and then we'll further deal with the matter. We take a break first after the witness has left the courtroom. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Meanwhile, I use the time for the following. It's about the Prosecution using documents during the Defence case. During the testimony of Milenko Indjic, the Defence complained that certain documents used by the Prosecution during cross-examination had not been disclosed or were not properly added to its Rule 65 ter exhibit list. This and the ensuing discussion can be found at transcript pages 25154 up to 25164.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers the matter to be resolved but further points the parties to a decision in the Stanisic and Simatovic case of the 26th of August 2011 where this matter is further analysed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But before beginning, I just wanted to let the Chamber know that Mr. Stojanovic did communicate to me the eight documents -- actually, in addition to the statement, that being the ninth, that were being tendered, and I will then just, if it's okay with the Chamber, tender any additional documents during the course of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will go through this list after the -- but could you already indicate, Mr. Weber, whether there are objections to be expected in relation to the documents now highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections to the documents that are highlighted. However, I will further discuss with Mr. Stojanovic, and I mention a paragraph with respect to the statement that we may oppose because of the absence of associated exhibits being tendered with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One correction I would like to put on the record. Mr. Stojanovic, the witness statement which was MFI'd earlier this morning, D641, has a different 65 ter number than you indicated in your list. The right number is 1D4096. This is what we noticed by Madam Registrar. Could you please check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do see that on the list now that we have the statement of the witness twice, first on the first category, statement, and then again with the associated exhibits. And there, as just indicated by Judge Fluegge, with the wrong 65 ter number which has now been corrected on the record and which you are invited to verify. Mr. Vujasin, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution and you find him to your right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vujasin.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit 353, page 29 of the B/C/S original and page 28 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you will be a 30 May 1992 entry from one of General Mladic's notebooks concerning a meeting with unit commanders of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I'll wait for this to come before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could have page 29 of the original in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this entry next to item number 2 on this page, we see your name and it is noted that you are the commander of the 1st Lpbr in Rajlovac. Is it correct that this was your position at the end of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, under 2, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is this the meeting that you have been discussing today that was held in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes. I just didn't know that it was a Saturday, the day of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, was this the only meeting that you attended with General Mladic between May and September 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I didn't have any other meetings until I came to the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. There were no more of these meetings until the 15th or 16th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's understood. Throughout this meeting, the various brigade commanders report on matters in their respective zones of operations. Some include, as you can see even under Colonel Milosevic's entry, the amount of persons which appear to be under their command as part of their reports. In the parenthesis under your name in item 2, it states: "(About 850)". On this date is it correct that you reported to General Mladic that there were about 850 individuals under your command?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: It says here 850 but it's 850 who could have been placed at disposal in Rajlovac, those who could bear arms and who were subject to military service. But most of them were useless, this included the president of the municipality on, so it was the number that could be gathered. These were not people who actually bore weapons but it was the number that could be made available.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to speak louder and into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I then understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak a bit louder and could you please speak more into the microphone. I see the microphone is directed quite far away from ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 850 given here in parentheses, these were men that were in the entire territory of the Rajlovac municipality that was subject to military duty but that number was never actually under weapons and engaged in the Rajlovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that number in a later document that we'll look at, but I'd like to show you one more page in this notebook while we're here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could have page 35 of the B/C/S original and page 34 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This relates to a meeting that you were not present for or a conversation that you were not present for which appeared to occur after your meeting, according to the notebook, in the afternoon on the 30th. It relates to a conversation with Colonel Wilson. The notes state: "Secretary-General asked him to convey you a message as soon as possible: for the shelling of Sarajevo to stop and to express his concern at the destruction of Sarajevo." Sir, I put it to you that there was destruction being caused to Sarajevo due to shelling by the VRS around the time of your meeting. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know that data. I'm not sure about this. I really am not able to give you an answer on this. What I can say is that there was no shooting from the area of responsibility of Rajlovac at the city of Sarajevo. That's what I can state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll go in further into the activities of your brigade at this time. Right now I'd like to move on to a couple other small items.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said what you can say is that there was no shooting from the area of responsibility of Rajlovac, what time-frame do you have in mind was there no shooting? And you're looking at Mr. Weber, but this question is put to you by me as the Presiding Judge. Could you tell us what time you had on your mind that there was no shooting? Was it for months? Was it for years? Was it for days? And if so, what years, what months, or what days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this part that refers to the meeting, that refers to the meeting that was held, and so this is the report for the afternoon. There was no shooting at the town then. It was not possible because based on what I learned later, the attack on Osijek, the Butile barracks, took place so that there was shooting from Ahatovici at positions where the Rajlovac Brigade was located, so I'm saying that it wasn't possible that there was any fire directed at the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that cover the previous days, the days before Colonel Wilson comes and asks to stop the shelling? Was there no shooting in the days, well, let's say the week before Colonel Wilson met with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really -- I can't say. I can't say. There was firing. On the 4th of April Rajlovac barracks was attacked, so there was fire in defence as of the 4th of April when the barracks was attacked. So until the 13th, this firing was constant. From time to time, it was from both sides. Not three or four days would pass without some form of fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And after the 13th? Because this meeting was held on the 30th of May, which is six weeks later, what happened in those six weeks as far as shooting is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I understood the question. Could the interpreter repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I will repeat the question. I asked you about the time-frame of where you said that there had been no shooting from the Rajlovac Brigade. I asked you whether that extended to a time period before the 30th of May. You then explained that between the 4th and the 13th of April, there had been shooting in the context of an attack to the barracks. What I'm asking you now is whether there was any firing from the Rajlovac Brigade between the 13th of April and the date of this meeting which was the 30th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was firing by members of the Rajlovac Brigade who came there from Mijatovica Kosa, from their homes. I remember very well these were people who had fled from their homes, they came to the barracks in Rajlovac, they were staying there, and they were watching as the items from their houses were being taken out. There were mortars there that were left from the time of the JNA, and there was a soldier who was very upset at what he was seeing going on in his house and he went to the mortars and he fired out of anger because of the appliances and things that were being taken out of their houses. So there was fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just that one incident or more frequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I know about, that incident I'm aware of. I know of that incident. However, it's possible that there was something coming from the other areas. The line was established from Vogosca Brigade, behind the depot, it lay -- that's where the line was established, so I cannot say. It was either some firing from there or from elsewhere, so there was intermittent firing in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But not from Rajlovac if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the barracks. If you're thinking of from the barracks, then no, there was none as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 1D04089. This is a document that's referred to in paragraph 76 of the witness's statement, and I'm going to use it quickly just because it was not indicated as one of the associated exhibits that Mr. Stojanovic intended to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 15 June 1992 SRK 1st lmBR Rajlovac request from you as the commander of the brigade. Is it correct that you continued as the commander of the Rajlovac Brigade until the 15th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Correct. I carried out that duty after Doljanic Rajko left and before my successor came.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll clarify this. Sir, your successor was Mr. Milos Golijanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this document, what does the 1st lmBr stand for?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: We named it ourselves. We wanted to have mechanised equipment and I asked various organs that a tank company be transferred here so that we could secure that area and that is why we named it light mechanised brigade, but such a brigade does not exist by establishment. It was our creation and it was formed from the assets that were left in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4089 receives number P6744, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just as a housekeeping matter on that, I see that that document, there's a duplicate of it on the Prosecution 65 ter list under 11917, just so we prevent the re-tendering of that later. Could the Prosecution please have 1D04082. This is referred to in paragraph 74 of the witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Vujasin, this is a 6 June 1992 order from the Vogosca Operations Group Commander, Vukota Vukovic. Is it correct that Colonel Vukovic was commander of this operations group in June of 1992 and into the fall of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Colonel Vukota Vukovic was a professor in Rajlovac. At the beginning of the conflict he was in Vogosca securing the Vogosca bridge, and then when the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew on the 13th from Rajlovac he remained --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- sorry to interrupt you, but I would like to proceed efficiently through your examination. There's no need to provide a whole history of each individual I discuss with you. If you could please focus on my questions. Is it correct that Colonel Vukovic was the commander of the Vogosca operations group in June 1992 and continued in this position for the rest of that year?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Well it's difficult to say yes or no. The operations group is formed for specific tasks. I don't know if he had an order to be there but he was the most senior officer, so there was an order and he could have unified that eastern part, and this happened in 1993 or 1994 when the 3rd Sarajevo Brigade was formed. In other words, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go through this order a little bit. In the first paragraph, Colonel Vukovic appoints Miladin Trifunovic and sets forth a series of tasks. The order states: "His task will be to maintain and fully fortify current positions and establish the firing system in accordance with national positions and the line of defence." "He will keep one-third of the troops in the state of permanent readiness, prepare the unit for combat, train the units to handle heavy artillery weapons, and soldiers to handle personal weapons, move on the ground, and camouflage." The next item, number 2, appears to relate to you. It's an appointment designating you as -- mentioning you as commander of the brigade. And then it states that your tasks will be the same as those above which appears to relate to those of Captain Trifunovic. Do you see this information? Have I understood this order correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 42 of your statement in this case, you state: "The Rajlovac Brigade did not have heavy weapons, those larger than 82-millimetres." This appointment appears to indicate that one of your tasks was to train units to handle heavy artillery weapons. Could you please explain the reason Colonel Vukovic would assign you to train your units to handle heavy artillery if you did not have them?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: This was a general assignment issued to Miladin to avoid repetition from item 2 and item 1, so the training was to be on what I had and to have a third of the men in reserve in case of any negative situations, God forbid. This was perhaps a general order and perhaps he did not have information about everything that we had at our disposal. I must note that Rajlovac was a base so you didn't know what was left behind, what was taken out, where what was. Perhaps the when weaponry had gone to the anti-aircraft defence. We don't know if the JNA took it because it went through Vogosca. Perhaps he had pulled everything out to Stupska or the 5th Vogosca. So I really wasn't sure about the status.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that in the time, your time in the Rajlovac Brigade that you did have weaponry over 82-millimetres in calibre? I put it to you that you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would it not be fair to read to the witness the line following the line you read about the 82-millimetres, starting at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, very well, Your Honour. And I'm sorry if I confused my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Maybe if you could just help us understand your statement here. "There were problems with ammunition and we were always short of it, particularly of artillery ammunition. The Rajlovac Brigade did not have heavy weapons, those larger than 82-millimetres. At the beginning, we had three or four 82-millimetre mortars."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I read 120, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, I -- yes, thank you, Your Honour. You're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- reading better than me this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "... four 120-millimetre mortars." And I just want to stop there. I'll address the snipers in a little bit. Sir, so actually what I'm putting to you is that you did have heavy weapons larger than 82-millimetres; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: There were three mortars or four, I don't know exactly, that stayed in the barracks in Rajlovac. So there were three or four of them. Then there were 82-millimetre mortars, part of them. So that was it. Now, I don't know whether anything is being transferred here. In the former JNA, 120-millimetre mortars were transferred to the infantry. Now I cannot say but at any rate it was three or four of these mortars. When people say artillery ammunition, that is what is meant. That is my understanding of that. That's this first period. I mean, later --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well just before we leave this document, you also referred -- it also refers to training of personal weapons. Is it correct that the Rajlovac Brigade possessed M-76 and M-48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: That is correct. That is correct. An entire warehouse full of ammunition and weapons stayed on and I know that we distributed that to Serbs and Muslims and I know that that unit had these rifles, so -- so they did have these weapons. Now -- oh, yes, that's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I want -- when you say they had these weapons, you're referring to your brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Let's think this up: The base as the base had this, the brigade had this. Now, the personnel who had it then, they got it. I don't know how familiar you are with Rajlovac. I'm sure that you looked at the map during these preparations. This was a transit zone and everybody who went through there, they got their weapons from Rajlovac. And according to the order of Vukota Vukovic, the Kosevo Brigade was trained up, Rajlovac, because then this regiment came from Zadar at the time, so there were all sorts of -- well, I mean, there were these light weapons -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now just focusing on this order, you carried it out; correct? You did training on personal weapons including the M-76s and M-48 rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Well, quite a few people knew about this and I know that later, a sergeant who had come from Serbia, I mean everybody who was gathered there in Rajlovac, 18-year-olds who hadn't served their term in the military, we organised this training. We made this plan for like one month and in order to have people trained so that they would not just lose their lives and basically in the barracks or wherever they may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that some of your men mounted optical sights on top of some of these rifles as parts of their personal weapons kits?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Well, now, these optical sights, they were manufactured in Zrak. In Zrak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I didn't ask where they were manufactured or anything like that. A very straightforward question: Is it correct that some of your men mounted optical sights on top of some of these rifles as part of their personal weapons kit?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct. They had this -- these optical sites. I mean they had left the area of responsibility. Now, how that stayed there, I mean we have to go back to the previous thing. I mean, that is to say that this was obtained even before the war. But optical sights were not being distributed by these officers who stayed on in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. This Chamber has received evidence that these kind of rifles could be used by snipers. I put it to you that in the vicinity of your brigade, there were individuals who were provided with training on how to use M-76 and M-48 rifles, thereby individuals who were trained to use these weapons, and your statement is not accurate that there was no trained professional snipers. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I cannot agree. As far as I know, no training was conducted. It is possible that somebody may have organised training. I mean if they had a rifle, if they did it somewhere else, I cannot deny that. But I just know that there was no organised training for this kind of activity; that is to say, these young soldiers took their oath on St. Vitus's day on the 28th of June. The Commander Vukota Vukovic, I mean, that was in this hall in Rajlovac, that's where they took the oath and that's where we started training. I mean, they'd take the oath and then they'd move on and train with Jovic. I think that was the name of the sergeant. So that was not that. Now, these were young people. Now whether anybody had come from the army before that, I mean infantry units, police, things like that, I cannot say whether somebody like that trained people, but I'm saying this because this was not organised by the Superior Command or this operative group Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honours, I'm not going to tender this document since Mr. Stojanovic has indicated that this was one of the associated exhibits he wanted. I'm going to move on, actually to -- could the Prosecution please have P4357 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, Witness, your statement contains the Rajlovac Brigade had no trained professional snipers. If I understood your testimony well, you do not exclude for the possibility that people within the brigade had been trained, although not organised by you, in the use of rifles and that optical sites may have been mounted on the rifles that were within the brigade. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In those circumstances, I would say the Rajlovac Brigade had no trained professional snipers is not a very accurate statement of the situation within the brigade. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a 25 June 1992 request from Colonel Hasic, the SRK assistant commander for logistics, to the VRS Main Staff Koran command post. The order states: "Based on the conversation with General Mladic, the commander of the army of the SR BiH, we hereby ask you to provide the following equipment for the needs of the Rajlovac Brigade." Included in the request is eight snipers. Do I understand this correctly that this refers to eight sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I think that this 50 camouflage uniforms -- well, yes, it's the corps command that is asking the Main Staff. Probably it was for us because we had a lot of deaths in front of the kitchen door. People would get hit right here and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, we'll go through this. I'm just asking you very simple to clarify do you agree that the reference to eight snipers refers to eight sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the witness confirmed, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and pistols down here. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that such a request for the needs of the Rajlovac Brigade would have come up from you as a commanding officer in the brigade through the SRK command to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: This is the 25th of June, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that's the day of the document.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Well, I think a month or a month and a half before that, Golijanin came who took over. I think that this is not my request, possibly his or there's also --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Soldiers were asking for this to be done to prevent all these deaths in Rajlovac. There is such a lot of sniper fire. We have nothing to respond with. It's from the Rajlovac Brigade at any rate. Yes, otherwise they won't ask for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when Milos Golijanin took over the brigade you remained the deputy commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Yes, I stayed there until the 15th, until the 15th of September. Now this, the 25th, no, sorry -- sorry, then it went from us. From us, yes, when I held that position. Sorry, I thought it was the 9th. Sorry. Sorry. I got a bit confused in terms of dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could I seek clarification. Earlier you said, talking about this same request, that you referred to a date and you said: "I think that this is not my request, possibly his or there's also ..." Now, I know that you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that you have corrected yourself but the interpreters could not hear the last name you mentioned. So apart from referring to yourself and to Mr. Golijanin, could you tell us what other name you mentioned when you said "or there's also ..." and you then mentioned a name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Logistics organs, possibly logistics organs because they asked for pistols and everything else. These people who are in Rajlovac; that is to say, I mean from logistics. From the logistics people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have clarified and you have filled in what the interpreters could not hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just get clarification further. Now that you have corrected yourself on the dates, is it correct therefore that this request was yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally cannot say that I sent this, but most probably from the logistics organs of the Rajlovac Brigade. It would be the corps commander if it went through the corps command, so that would have been in stronger terms. This came from the logistics organs. I assumed that we got these rifles -- I mean within some units, something would be formed so that we could organise appropriate activity. I mean, I have to say that we did not receive this although a request had been sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31254.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, coming up before you will be a 27 July 1992 request from Milos Golijanin the commander of the Rajlovac Brigade. The request at the beginning states: "We hereby inform you that with respect to the number of soldiers and the types of weapons in the unit, we have in our possession the necessary number of bk combat sets for specific weapons and artillery pieces except for the following types of ammunition and MES which we need you to approve for our replenishment." Under item 2, this request asks for 9.000 7.9-millimetre sniper rounds. Do you see this information?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I put it to you that your brigade would not have requested so many sniper rounds if it did not have snipers to use these weapons. Do you agree that by this time you had people using weapons for these calibre rounds?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: This sniper, this sniper bullets, no M-48 rifles, M-76 that the brigade had, so it used those bullets and they work better and they had sights. But it's not a sniper rifle. It's with optical sights that they improve precision, and then there wouldn't be a waste of ammunition. And this is three or four boxes, so I don't know exactly how many are in one box so that's why this was asked for. And from there you can see that in fact we didn't have this ammunition, and then he asked for replenishment so that he'd have all of it. I see down here this other ammunition too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd asked my question on the document. I would tender it into evidence and I see that we're at a break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do that, I just want to say: Witness, you say that these were not sniper rifles, but I see at item 17 of this request there's also a request for eight sniper rifles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I assume that that was asked for that -- I mean, that's correct, well, nothing else, well, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. Witness, would you please -- you want to tender the document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, please. [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness can already follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31254 receives number P6745, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you'd like I can read out the next document that I'll be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution will be calling up 65 ter 31253.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, I think I had not yet -- no, I'll leave it until later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is a 24 September 1992 request from Colonel Vukovic asking Pretis to supply 30 120-millimetre light contact fuse motors and 40 105-millimetre shells to the Rajlovac Brigade. Is it correct 105-millimetre shells are heavy artillery ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: 105-millimetres, is that what you mean? The one down here, 40 pieces, 105-millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, yes, that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: I think that this is for artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Which begs the question: which artillery pieces did you have or is it correct that you had 105-millimetre howitzers in your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: Forty pieces. Now, is this combat kit? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. The question was whether you had 105-millimetre howitzers in your brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time of this request, I don't think so, but it could have come from - what was its name? - Ilijas. It could have come from Ilijas, from other units. It could have been done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to put it to you that you are minimising your evidence related to the artillery in your brigade and that you did, in fact, have artillery pieces greater than 82-millimetres. Do you have any other comments?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: No, I don't think it can be that way. There was this problem of ammunition. And also this artillery ammunition, when that was being asked for, the brigades were linked up. The Rajlovac Brigade did not have any, I know that. So Vukota Vukovic, this is the 24th of September, if you had ammunition it was easy to get weapons from another unit 10 kilometres maximum, that was the distance. That's why I'm saying, I am not minimising what you are saying but I cannot confirm it either. We did not have our own weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question here. Sir, just before this disappears from the page, at page 46, line 6, you are asked a question: "Is it correct 105-millimetre shells are heavy artillery ammunition?" You haven't answered that question. Can you answer with a yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so, yes, that ammunition --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just on the answer you gave, it's really not clear what you're saying to me. Did you get heavy artillery weapons from other units? Were there occasions when that happened? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can you hear the English booth now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you now. Witness, could you please repeat your answer. The question again because we didn't receive interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you get heavy artillery weapons from other units?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO VUJASIN
utterances.text: This is what I was saying.
